summary: We develop graph neural networks for molecular property prediction, focusing on the low-data regime. Our main interest is transfer learning and pretraining strategies that let a model trained on large public molecule corpora adapt to small proprietary assay datasets (hundreds of labeled molecules), together with calibrated uncertainty estimates so that chemists know when to distrust a prediction.

claims.text: We pretrain a message-passing graph neural network on five million unlabeled molecules using masked-atom prediction combined with a contextual subgraph objective, and show this initialization transfers to downstream assays.

We fine-tune the pretrained encoder on proprietary assay sets containing between 200 and 800 labels using low-rank adapters, updating under two percent of the parameters rather than the full backbone.
We claim that adapter-based fine-tuning helps mainly by reducing variance across random seeds, and that its improvement in mean absolute error is smaller than previously reported.
We obtain calibrated uncertainty estimates by wrapping a deep ensemble in split conformal prediction, and show this restores nominal interval coverage on held-out scaffolds.
We show that deep ensembles remain systematically overconfident under scaffold split unless they are conformalized, which we argue is the dominant failure mode in deployment.
We claim that curating the pretraining corpus by chemical-space overlap with the downstream task matters more for transfer than increasing the size of the pretraining corpus.
We use uncertainty-guided batch active learning with the calibrated model as surrogate, and report roughly forty percent fewer assays to reach a target hit rate compared with random acquisition.

We transfer from abundant low-fidelity computational labels to scarce high-fidelity experimental assay labels in a multi-fidelity setup, treating the low-fidelity signal as an auxiliary pretraining task.
We propose a latent-space distance diagnostic that predicts when the uncertainty estimates of the model will lose coverage, and use it as a gate before committing screening resources.
We argue that random splits overstate transfer to novel chemical series, and we report all results under scaffold split with explicit chemical-similarity statistics.
